sourceText: - **251.** Researchers trust small samples too much, the "law of small numbers" (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971).
title: A small sample feels certain
lens: the sampling spread hidden by a point estimate

sourceText: - **252.** Most people said a small and a large hospital equally often record days with over 60% boys; the small one does far more often (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972).
title: Two maternity wards
lens: a strict sixty-percent tail in unequal samples

sourceText: - **254.** Under time pressure, people who see a technology as beneficial also see it as low-risk, an affect heuristic (Finucane et al., 2000).
title: Benefit colors the risk estimate
lens: the weight given to a favorable cue

sourceText: - **255.** New stocks with easy-to-pronounce names or tickers outperformed others shortly after listing (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2006).
title: A name and an early return
lens: a descriptive return contrast without a causal conclusion

sourceText: - **257.** People gave $2.38 on average to help one named girl, Rokia, but $1.14 after reading statistics on millions in need (Small, Loewenstein & Slovic, 2007).
title: One story, two donation averages
lens: the denominator behind mean donations

sourceText: - **258.** A single identified child drew more donations than a group of eight (Kogut & Ritov, 2005).
title: One child or a group?
lens: total versus per-recipient giving in an explicit example

sourceText: - **259.** Money pours into mutual funds after strong past returns, but leaves poor performers only slowly (Sirri & Tufano, 1998).
title: Money follows the fund
lens: the asymmetry of assumed inflows and outflows

sourceText: - **260.** Investors expect high returns after markets rise, even though high past returns predict lower future ones (Greenwood & Shleifer, 2014).
title: Forecast after a market rise
lens: the gap between a stated forecast and outcome

sourceText: - **261.** The Allais paradox: people's choices between gambles violate expected utility theory when a certain outcome is involved (Allais, 1953).
title: Cancel the common payoff
lens: a truly shared outcome in expected-cash arithmetic

sourceText: - **262.** People prefer bets with known odds over unknown odds, even when unknown odds are no worse (Ellsberg, 1961).
title: Known odds, unknown odds
lens: the expectation bounds left by ambiguous odds

sourceText: - **263.** People overweight small probabilities and underweight large ones, an inverse-S curve (Tversky & Kahneman, 1992; Prelec, 1998).
title: Probability and decision weight
lens: a nonlinear decision-weight curve

sourceText: - **264.** Lower-income households spend a larger share of income on lottery tickets (Clotfelter & Cook, 1990).
title: Lottery spending as income share
lens: the income denominator with fixed spending

sourceText: - **265.** Long shots at the racetrack are overbet and favorites underbet (Griffith, 1949), mainly from misjudged probabilities (Snowberg & Wolfers, 2010).
title: A long shot at what price?
lens: the actual win probability behind betting value

sourceText: - **267.** People would pay $14.12 for flight insurance against terrorism but only $12.03 for insurance against any cause (Johnson, Hershey, Meszaros & Kunreuther, 1993).
title: Coverage for any cause
lens: the covered event and the premium together

sourceText: - **269.** Emotionally vivid prizes, like a kiss from a film star, make people less sensitive to probability (Rottenstreich & Hsee, 2001).
title: A vivid prize and its odds
lens: a deliberately flattened probability-weight model

sourceText: - **270.** Expected utility theory cannot explain why people turn down small favorable bets without implying absurd behavior for large ones (Rabin, 2000).
title: A favorable bet and wealth
lens: the wealth assumption behind utility curvature

sourceText: - **272.** Risk aversion rises when stakes are scaled up (Holt & Laury, 2002).
title: Scale the same lottery
lens: stakes relative to fixed wealth

sourceText: - **273.** *Deal or No Deal* contestants took more risk after bad luck, consistent with break-even seeking (Post, van den Assem, Baltussen & Thaler, 2008).
title: Chasing the break-even point
lens: the expected payoff separate from a desired target

sourceText: - **274.** Investors put most of their money in domestic stocks despite diversification gains abroad (French & Poterba, 1991).
title: Home holdings and covariance
lens: the diversification channel under specified covariance

sourceText: - **275.** 73% of men but 35% of women chose to compete in a tournament, despite equal performance (Niederle & Vesterlund, 2007).
title: Who enters the tournament?
lens: the denominator in descriptive participation rates

sourceText: - **277.** Indonesian villagers recently hit by floods or earthquakes became more risk-averse (Cameron & Shah, 2015).
title: Risk after a recent disaster
lens: an assumed change in sensitivity after a shock

sourceText: - **278.** People who lived through poor stock returns take less financial risk for decades afterward (Malmendier & Nagel, 2011).
title: Which return history gets weight?
lens: the weight of personal experience in a toy forecast

sourceText: - **279.** Fearful people judge risks higher, while angry people judge them lower (Lerner & Keltner, 2001).
title: Fear and the starting estimate
lens: the cue entering a risk-judgment rule

sourceText: - **280.** Morning sunshine in a stock exchange's city is linked to higher daily returns (Hirshleifer & Shumway, 2003).
title: Sunshine and group composition
lens: a descriptive association sensitive to composition

sourceText: - **282.** Because people read the leftmost digit first, $2.99 vs $3.00 feels like a bigger gap than $4.00 vs $4.01 (Thomas & Morwitz, 2005).
title: Across the left digit
lens: equal cash gaps with unequal integer-part changes

sourceText: - **283.** Women's clothing priced at $39 outsold the same item at $34 or $44 (Anderson & Simester, 2003).
title: Price ending and revenue
lens: quantity and margin in a price comparison

sourceText: - **284.** Cutting a price to zero raises demand far more than an equal cut between two positive prices (Shampanier, Mazar & Ariely, 2007).
title: The price reaches zero
lens: unit economics even when assumed demand rises

sourceText: - **286.** Firms can profit by hiding add-on fees from inattentive buyers, and competition may not stop it (Gabaix & Laibson, 2006).
title: The hidden add-on
lens: the complete price after add-on fees

sourceText: - **288.** Posting tax-inclusive prices on shelves cut demand for taxed items about 8% (Chetty, Looney & Kroft, 2009).
title: A tax-inclusive shelf label
lens: the baseline behind a stated relative demand change

sourceText: - **289.** eBay buyers underweight shipping charges, so higher shipping with lower prices raises revenue (Hossain & Morgan, 2006).
title: Bid price plus shipping
lens: equal final bills with unequal price components

sourceText: - **290.** "Pay what you want" with half going to charity raised profits on souvenir photos (Gneezy, Gneezy, Nelson & Brown, 2010).
title: Half the photo price to charity
lens: donations and sales costs in profit

sourceText: - **291.** Access to buy-now-pay-later raised total spending (Di Maggio, Katz & Williams, 2022).
title: Installments still add up
lens: the total cash commitment behind small installments

sourceText: - **292.** Cookies from a nearly empty jar were rated more desirable than identical cookies from a full one (Worchel, Lee & Adewole, 1975).
title: A scarce-looking cookie jar
lens: unit quantity separate from a scarcity cue

sourceText: - **293.** Shoppers react more to prices above their reference price than to equal prices below it (Kalyanaram & Winer, 1995).
title: A price above the reference
lens: the sign of a price difference under a stated value rule

sourceText: - **294.** Brand choice data show loss aversion: price rises hurt sales more than equal cuts help (Hardie, Johnson & Fader, 1993).
title: Equal changes, different slopes
lens: an explicitly asymmetric response rule

sourceText: - **295.** Penny auctions earn sellers far more than item value as bidders chase sunk costs (Augenblick, 2016).
title: Every bid has a fee
lens: the accumulated bid fees in an auction bill

sourceText: - **296.** Many consumers pick flat-rate internet plans even when pay-per-use would cost less (Lambrecht & Skiera, 2006).
title: The flat plan versus usage
lens: the usage threshold in a plan comparison

sourceText: - **297.** Buyers of extended warranties overestimate how often products fail (Abito & Salant, 2019).
title: The warranty break-even point
lens: the failure probability needed to cover the premium

sourceText: - **298.** Posting unit-price lists in supermarkets moved shoppers toward cheaper products (Russo, 1977).
title: Compare the shelf units
lens: the common quantity denominator

sourceText: - **299.** Viewed alone, 7 oz of ice cream overflowing a small cup was valued more ($2.26) than 8 oz in a large cup ($1.66) (Hsee, 1998).
title: Cup size and actual ice cream
lens: the price per stated ounce

sourceText: - **302.** Small payments lowered performance on IQ questions and charity collection compared with no payment, "pay enough or don't pay at all" (Gneezy & Rustichini, 2000).
title: A small payment with a cost
lens: a stated participation cost alongside a reward

sourceText: - **303.** Swiss residents' support for a local nuclear waste site fell from 50.8% to 24.6% when compensation was offered (Frey & Oberholzer-Gee, 1997).
title: Compensation and recorded support
lens: the denominator in observed support shares

sourceText: - **304.** Paying for blood reduced women's donations, unless the payment could be given to charity (Mellström & Johannesson, 2008).
title: Payment passed to charity
lens: the destination of a payment in cash accounting

sourceText: - **306.** Children promised a reward for drawing later drew less in free time than unrewarded children (Lepper, Greene & Nisbett, 1973).
title: Reward now, activity later
lens: a specified activity path rather than a universal reward effect

sourceText: - **307.** A meta-analysis found expected tangible rewards reduce intrinsic motivation for interesting tasks (Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999), a finding disputed by Cameron & Pierce (1994).
title: Rewards and conflicting evidence
lens: the sensitivity of a pooled estimate to included evidence

sourceText: - **308.** In India, very large bonuses relative to pay worsened performance on several tasks (Ariely, Gneezy, Loewenstein & Mazar, 2009).
title: A bigger performance bonus
lens: output versus payment in a toy incentive budget

sourceText: - **310.** UK fruit pickers' productivity rose at least 50% when pay switched from relative to individual piece rates (Bandiera, Barankay & Rasul, 2005).
title: A new piece-rate baseline
lens: the absolute increase behind a relative productivity change

sourceText: - **311.** Public recognition beat financial rewards for Zambian hairdressers selling condoms (Ashraf, Bandiera & Jack, 2014).
title: Recognition and program cost
lens: the cost denominator in a reward comparison

sourceText: - **313.** Paying students to visit the gym eight times in a month roughly doubled their attendance in later weeks (Charness & Gneezy, 2009).
title: Attendance after the reward
lens: the starting attendance behind doubling

sourceText: - **314.** Lottery and deposit-contract incentives helped people lose about 13–14 lb in 16 weeks versus about 4 lb in controls, though much was regained (Volpp et al., 2008).
title: Initial loss and later regain
lens: the retained amount after a specified reversal

sourceText: - **315.** Paying smokers up to $750 to quit raised long-term quit rates from 5.0% to 14.7% (Volpp et al., 2009).
title: Quit rates and absolute gaps
lens: absolute rates rather than a relative headline

sourceText: - **316.** Daily lottery incentives improved adherence to the blood thinner warfarin (Volpp et al., 2008).
title: An adherence lottery budget
lens: the expected payment under an explicit lottery rule

sourceText: - **317.** Specific, challenging goals raise performance more than "do your best" (Locke & Latham, 2002).
title: A concrete output target
lens: the rate required to reach a stated goal

sourceText: - **318.** Performance pay for Indian teachers raised test scores 0.27 SD in math and 0.17 SD in language after two years (Muralidharan & Sundararaman, 2011).
title: Math and language in SD units
lens: two outcomes expressed on a specified common scale

sourceText: - **319.** Camera monitoring plus pay tied to attendance cut teacher absence in Rajasthan from 42% to 21% (Duflo, Hanna & Ryan, 2012).
title: Absence and attendance
lens: the difference between absence and its complement

sourceText: - **320.** A purely symbolic award raised workers' performance about 12% (Kosfeld & Neckermann, 2011).
title: A symbolic award, a baseline
lens: the base behind a stated twelve-percent change

sourceText: - **321.** Save More Tomorrow, where workers commit future raises to savings, lifted saving rates from 3.5% to 13.6% over 40 months (Thaler & Benartzi, 2004).
title: Save a share of future raises
lens: the savings allocation rule for future salary increases

sourceText: - **322.** About 85% of Danes are passive savers whose savings follow employer defaults rather than tax incentives (Chetty, Friedman, Leth-Petersen, Nielsen & Olsen, 2014).
title: Passive savers and defaults
lens: the retained default among an assumed passive share

sourceText: - **323.** In the same data, automatic contributions raised total savings far more per dollar of public cost than tax subsidies (Chetty et al., 2014).
title: Saving per public-cost unit
lens: net saving after a stated program cost

sourceText: - **324.** Only about a third of Americans over 50 answered three basic questions on interest, inflation and diversification correctly (Lusardi & Mitchell, 2011).
title: Three questions, a denominator
lens: the descriptive share behind a literacy score

sourceText: - **325.** Financial education explained about 0.1% of the variation in financial behavior, and effects faded within about 20 months (Fernandes, Lynch & Netemeyer, 2014).
title: A small explained share
lens: the difference between correlation and explained variation

sourceText: - **326.** **\[contested\]** A later meta-analysis of randomized trials found larger effects, similar to other education programs (Kaiser, Lusardi, Menkhoff & Urban, 2022).
title: A different trial collection
lens: the evidence mix behind conflicting pooled estimates

sourceText: - **327.** People underestimate compound growth, and those who do so most borrow more and save less (Stango & Zinman, 2009).
title: The growth that compounds
lens: the horizon of compound growth

sourceText: - **329.** About 29% of credit card accounts regularly pay at or near the minimum (Keys & Wang, 2019).
title: Accounts near the minimum
lens: the account count behind a percentage

sourceText: - **330.** Many households carry high-interest card debt while holding low-yield cash (Gross & Souleles, 2002).
title: Debt beside low-yield cash
lens: the interest-rate spread on both balance-sheet sides

sourceText: - **332.** Prize-linked savings accounts in South Africa raised savings and lowered lottery spending (Cole, Iverson & Tufano, 2022).
title: A prize-linked savings budget
lens: the expected prize cost per explicit account

sourceText: - **334.** Employees overinvest in their own company's stock, especially after it has done well (Benartzi, 2001).
title: The employer in the fund menu
lens: the exposure induced by an allocation menu

sourceText: - **335.** About 60% of Enron's 401(k) assets were in Enron stock before its collapse.
title: One employer dominates savings
lens: the loss exposure from a specified concentrated holding

sourceText: - **336.** When offered only one commitment account, people deposited more in the version with the higher early-withdrawal penalty (Beshears, Choi, Harris, Laibson, Madrian & Sakong, 2020).
title: A commitment withdrawal penalty
lens: the cost of an early exit in a commitment contract

sourceText: - **337.** Survey questions that merely mentioned overdraft fees reduced overdrafts in the following months (Stango & Zinman, 2014).
title: Make overdraft fees visible
lens: the complete bill once a contingent fee is counted

sourceText: - **338.** Even staff given clear fee sheets mostly failed to pick the cheapest S&P 500 index fund (Choi, Laibson & Madrian, 2010).
title: The same index, different fees
lens: the compounding drag of a fee difference

sourceText: - **340.** About 20% of US households who should have refinanced their mortgage did not, losing a median of about $11,500 (Keys, Pope & Pope, 2016).
title: The refinance horizon
lens: the horizon needed to recover a switching cost

sourceText: - **341.** Video monitoring with real-time feedback raised ICU hand hygiene from under 10% to over 80% (Armellino et al., 2012).
title: Monitoring and recorded hygiene
lens: the denominator in a before-after descriptive contrast

sourceText: - **343.** In a megastudy of 19 text messages sent before doctor's appointments, saying a flu shot was "reserved for you" worked best (Milkman et al., 2021).
title: A reserved appointment message
lens: the reach and conversion of a stated reminder funnel

sourceText: - **345.** **\[contested\]** Ohio's COVID vaccine lottery showed no clear increase in vaccination in several analyses (Walkey, Law & Bosch, 2021).
title: A lottery estimate near zero
lens: the distinction between a tiny estimate and proof of an effect

sourceText: - **346.** Text reminders saying a COVID vaccine was "waiting for you" raised first-dose uptake by a few percentage points (Dai et al., 2021).
title: A few percentage points
lens: absolute uptake gaps under different denominators

sourceText: - **347.** Posting calories at New York Starbucks cut calories per transaction about 6% (Bollinger, Leslie & Sorensen, 2011).
title: Calories per transaction
lens: the starting calories behind a relative change

sourceText: - **348.** Philadelphia's soda tax cut taxed-drink volume about 38% after accounting for shopping outside the city (Roberto et al., 2019).
title: Volume after a tax
lens: the baseline and units behind a volume change

sourceText: - **349.** Graphic cigarette warnings outperform text-only warnings on attention and intentions to quit (Noar et al., 2016).
title: Attention is one funnel step
lens: attention versus the stated final action rate

sourceText: - **351.** In advance directives, 77% chose comfort care when it was the default, versus 43% when life-extending care was the default (Halpern et al., 2013).
title: Two advance-directive defaults
lens: the descriptive share under each stated default

sourceText: - **352.** Making generics the default in electronic prescribing raised generic prescribing from 75% to 98% (Patel et al., 2014).
title: Generic prescribing shares
lens: the denominator behind a prescribing-rate comparison

sourceText: - **353.** Lowering the default pill count for opioid prescriptions in health records reduced the number of pills prescribed (Delgado et al., 2018).
title: A prescription-count default
lens: the average count implied by a stated retention rule

sourceText: - **354.** Loss-framed incentives, where money is taken away for missing step goals, outperformed equal gain-framed rewards (Patel et al., 2016).
title: An incentive paid upfront
lens: the cash path versus the final cash balance

sourceText: - **355.** Paying employees to quit smoking worked better than free nicotine replacement or e-cigarettes, though absolute quit rates stayed low (Halpern et al., 2018).
title: A relative change from a low rate
lens: the absolute rates behind a large ratio

sourceText: - **356.** Doctors prescribe more antibiotics for respiratory infections as clinic sessions wear on (Linder et al., 2014).
title: A clinic session changes mix
lens: the patient mix behind a time-of-day association

sourceText: - **358.** Placebo pills given openly, with patients told they were placebos, still eased irritable bowel symptoms (Kaptchuk et al., 2010).
title: Open-label placebo arithmetic
lens: the spread needed to interpret a mean difference

sourceText: - **359.** Workplace commitment contracts improved long-run gym attendance for some employees (Royer, Stehr & Sydnor, 2015).
title: A gym commitment horizon
lens: the horizon over which a commitment cost is evaluated

sourceText: - **360.** A 25% rebate on healthy groceries raised the healthy share of purchases about 9% (An, 2013).
title: A healthy share grows nine percent
lens: relative share change versus percentage points

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **362.** Letters to Guatemalan taxpayers stressing honesty and norms raised tax declarations and payments (Kettle et al., 2016).
title: Letters reach only some taxpayers
lens: the reachable population in a stated response funnel

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **363.** Households with in-home electricity displays responded about three times as strongly to price spikes (Jessoe & Rapson, 2014).
title: Feedback and price response
lens: the assumed sensitivity to the same price signal

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **364.** Comparing households' water use to neighbors cut use about 4.8% in Georgia (Ferraro & Price, 2013).
title: Neighbor comparisons and water
lens: the water-use baseline behind a relative reduction

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **365.** Asking voters when, where and how they would vote raised turnout 4.1 points in single-voter households (Nickerson & Rogers, 2010).
title: Planning and turnout points
lens: the denominators behind an absolute turnout gap

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **366.** Simpler, clearer IRS notices raised take-up of the Earned Income Tax Credit (Bhargava & Manoli, 2015).
title: Simplify the notice
lens: the explicit reading burden of a form

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **368.** Text reminders over the summer after high school raised college enrollment about 3 points among low-income students (Castleman & Page, 2015).
title: Summer messages and enrollment
lens: percentage points and the enrollment denominator

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **369.** **\[contested\]** National-scale texting and mail nudges about college aid reaching 800,000 students had no effect (Bird et al., 2021).
title: A large reach with zero lift
lens: the difference between program reach and assumed incremental impact

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **370.** A reciprocity message ("If you needed a transplant, would you have one? If so, help others") added an estimated 100,000 UK organ-donor registrations a year (Behavioural Insights Team, 2013).
title: Scale a registration increment
lens: the population behind a projected registration count

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **372.** A 5-cent tax on disposable bags cut their use by over 40 points, while a 5-cent bonus for reusable bags had almost no effect (Homonoff, 2018).
title: A bag tax and a bag bonus
lens: the final monetary consequence of each label

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **373.** Text messages using a person's name raised payment of court fines from about 5% to 33% (Haynes, Green, Gallagher, John & Torgerson, 2013).
title: A name in the reminder
lens: the descriptive payment shares and their denominators

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **374.** Over 90% of Sacramento households stayed on time-of-use electricity pricing when it was the default, versus about 20% opting in, and default enrollees still cut peak use (Fowlie et al., 2021).
title: Time-of-use enrollment defaults
lens: the enrollment share implied by a stated retention rule

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **375.** Text reminders that named the borrower's loan officer improved microloan repayment (Karlan, Morten & Zinman, 2015).
title: Which borrower receives the text?
lens: reach separate from conditional repayment

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **376.** A Minnesota letter warning of an audit raised reported income for low and middle earners but lowered it for high earners (Slemrod, Blumenthal & Christian, 2001).
title: Opposite responses across groups
lens: heterogeneous group responses hidden in an aggregate

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **377.** Lowering office thermostats' default by 1°C lowered average settings by 0.38°C (Brown, Johnstone, Haščič, Vong & Barascud, 2013).
title: A colder thermostat default
lens: the assumed pass-through from default to selected setting

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **379.** Closing Social Security field offices cut disability applications in surrounding areas about 16% (Deshpande & Li, 2019).
title: An office closes, applications fall
lens: the baseline behind a relative application change

sourceSection: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceText: - **380.** Nudges like auto-enrollment often deliver more impact per dollar than traditional incentives such as tax credits (Benartzi et al., 2017).
title: Impact per program dollar
lens: the cost per specified incremental action

sourceText: - **382.** Indian data-entry workers chose contracts that penalized them for missing targets, and output rose about 6% (Kaur, Kremer & Mullainathan, 2015).
title: Output under a penalty contract
lens: the baseline behind an output increment

sourceText: - **383.** The same workers' output rose as payday approached (Kaur, Kremer & Mullainathan, 2015).
title: Effort as payday approaches
lens: the stipulated path of output toward payday

sourceText: - **384.** Managers avoid cutting pay mainly because they fear damage to morale (Bewley, 1999).
title: A pay cut and morale costs
lens: the asymmetric response assumed for equal pay changes

sourceText: - **386.** Indian farm wages rise after good harvests but rarely fall after bad ones (Kaur, 2019).
title: A wage that resists falling
lens: the sign of a wage relative to a reference

sourceText: - **387.** Job seekers in Hungary searched in ways consistent with comparing benefits to recent reference levels (DellaVigna, Lindner, Reizer & Schmieder, 2017).
title: Benefits and recent reference pay
lens: the reference wage behind a stated value comparison

sourceText: - **388.** Helping job seekers write a concrete search plan raised applications and job offers in South Africa (Abel, Burger, Carranza & Piraino, 2019).
title: Applications turn into offers
lens: search activity and conditional offer probabilities

sourceText: - **389.** Unemployed workers overestimate how quickly they'll find a job (Spinnewijn, 2015).
title: When will the job arrive?
lens: forecast probability versus a realized frequency

sourceText: - **390.** Their expectations barely fall as unemployment drags on, which helps explain long spells (Mueller, Spinnewijn & Topa, 2021).
title: A job-search belief barely moves
lens: the weight given to repeated unfavorable news

sourceText: - **391.** In one Carnegie Mellon cohort, 57% of men but 7% of women negotiated their first salary offer (Babcock & Laschever, 2003).
title: Who negotiates the first offer?
lens: the denominator behind a reported negotiation gap

sourceText: - **393.** Blind auditions behind a screen raised the odds of women advancing in orchestras (Goldin & Rouse, 2000). **\[contested\]** Critics argue the statistical evidence is weaker than often cited.
title: A blind-audition estimate varies
lens: the sensitivity of a contested pooled estimate

sourceText: - **394.** Resumes with white-sounding names got about 50% more callbacks than identical ones with Black-sounding names, 9.65% vs 6.45% (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004).
title: Callbacks with a common denominator
lens: absolute callback rates rather than a relative headline

sourceText: - **395.** In 83,000 applications to large US firms, white-sounding names got about 2 points more callbacks, concentrated in a small set of companies (Kline, Rose & Walters, 2022).
title: A gap concentrated in a few firms
lens: the firm weights behind an aggregate callback gap

sourceText: - **396.** Managers on fixed pay favored socially connected workers; with performance pay, they favored able ones (Bandiera, Barankay & Rasul, 2009).
title: Which worker attribute gets weight?
lens: the weighting rule for two applicant attributes

sourceText: - **397.** Working from home raised Chinese call-center performance 13% and halved quit rates (Bloom, Liang, Roberts & Ying, 2015).
title: Two work-from-home outcomes
lens: separate baselines and meanings of two reported changes

sourceText: - **399.** Telling workers their productivity rank raised output about 7% (Blanes i Vidal & Nossol, 2011).
title: Output after rank feedback
lens: the base behind a relative productivity increment

sourceText: - **400.** Fundraising callers who briefly met a scholarship student spent 142% more time on the phone and raised 171% more money (Grant et al., 2007).
title: Time and money are different outcomes
lens: two specified growth rates on a common toy baseline

sourceText: - **401.** Stock prices move far more than later dividends can justify (Shiller, 1981).
title: Price swings and cash-flow forecasts
lens: the numerical gap between prices and a stated benchmark

sourceText: - **402.** Portfolios of past 3–5-year losers beat past winners over the next 3–5 years (De Bondt & Thaler, 1985).
title: A past loser and a future return
lens: the separate periods in a return-reversal example

sourceText: - **403.** Stocks that rose over the past 3–12 months keep outperforming for several more months, momentum (Jegadeesh & Titman, 1993).
title: A momentum path is not certainty
lens: two possible next-period returns after the same past path

sourceText: - **404.** Prices keep drifting in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks afterward (Bernard & Thomas, 1989).
title: News enters the price gradually
lens: the remaining adjustment after a news signal

sourceText: - **406.** EntreMed's stock jumped over 300% after a front-page *New York Times* story on research published months earlier (Huberman & Regev, 2001).
title: An old story gets new attention
lens: the baseline behind a large price jump

sourceText: - **408.** Royal Dutch and Shell shares, with fixed claims on the same cash flows, traded far from their theoretical ratio for years (Froot & Dabora, 1999).
title: Two claims on one cash flow
lens: the observed price ratio versus a fixed claim ratio

sourceText: - **409.** After 3Com spun off part of Palm, markets valued 3Com's remaining business at a negative amount (Lamont & Thaler, 2003).
title: A negative implied stub
lens: the residual value after subtracting a separately priced stake

sourceText: - **410.** Firms that added ".com" to their names in 1998–99 saw large abnormal returns with no change in business (Cooper, Dimitrov & Rau, 2001).
title: A new name, a price change
lens: a descriptive price change with unchanged toy cash flows

sourceText: - **412.** Individual investors are net buyers of stocks in the news or with unusual volume (Barber & Odean, 2008).
title: News attracts a buying funnel
lens: attention separate from conditional purchasing

sourceText: - **413.** A national team's World Cup elimination is followed by a next-day stock market drop of about half a percentage point (Edmans, García & Norli, 2007).
title: A half-point daily market move
lens: the price baseline behind a percentage return

sourceText: - **414.** Mutual fund flows respond strongly to Morningstar star ratings (Del Guercio & Tkac, 2008).
title: Ratings and incoming fund money
lens: the assumed response funnel following a rating

sourceText: - **415.** The disposition effect among fund managers slows the reaction of prices to news (Frazzini, 2006).
title: The market adjusts slowly
lens: the adjustment speed in a stated price path

sourceText: - **416.** Robinhood users herd into stocks on its "top movers" lists, which then underperform (Barber, Huang, Odean & Schwarz, 2022).
title: A top-movers list draws a crowd
lens: list exposure separate from subsequent returns

sourceText: - **417.** Individual investors favor lottery-like stocks with low prices and high skew, especially lower-income investors (Kumar, 2009).
title: A stock with lottery-like payoffs
lens: the probability behind a skewed payoff expectation

sourceText: - **419.** Retirement-account logins fall after market drops (Sicherman, Loewenstein, Seppi & Utkus, 2016).
title: Market drops and account logins
lens: the denominator behind an attention count

sourceText: - **420.** In lab asset markets, bubbles and crashes form reliably until traders have been through them before (Smith, Suchanek & Williams, 1988).
title: A bubble and an assumed correction
lens: the stated adjustment path toward a valuation benchmark

sourceText: - **422.** Colonoscopy patients judged the experience by its worst and final moments; adding a gentler ending improved ratings and later return rates (Redelmeier & Kahneman, 1996; Redelmeier, Katz & Kahneman, 2003).
title: A gentler ending changes the summary
lens: the peak-end summary versus time-integrated discomfort

sourceText: - **423.** How long an experience lasts barely affects how it is remembered, duration neglect (Fredrickson & Kahneman, 1993).
title: Double the duration
lens: duration in total exposure but not an assumed memory rule

sourceText: - **424.** Lottery winners were not much happier than controls a year later, and accident victims recovered more than expected (Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman, 1978), though the samples were small.
title: A shock fades toward baseline
lens: the assumed persistence of a wellbeing shock

sourceText: - **426.** Day-to-day emotional wellbeing seemed to plateau around $75,000 income (Kahneman & Deaton, 2010); a joint reanalysis found it keeps rising for most people, plateauing only for the least happy 20% (Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers, 2023).
title: A plateau in one subgroup
lens: subgroup weights behind an aggregate income slope

sourceText: - **427.** Within countries richer people are happier, but national happiness did not rise with decades of growth, the Easterlin paradox (Easterlin, 1974).
title: Within-group and national averages
lens: composition separate from a within-group association

sourceText: - **428.** People given $5 or $20 to spend on others felt happier by evening than those told to spend it on themselves (Dunn, Aknin & Norton, 2008).
title: Money for self or someone else
lens: the remaining cash without scoring personal happiness

sourceText: - **429.** Spending on experiences brings more lasting happiness than spending on things (Van Boven & Gilovich, 2003).
title: Two assumed adaptation rates
lens: the persistence parameter in a toy experience model

sourceText: - **431.** Assistant professors overestimated how unhappy being denied tenure would make them (Gilbert, Pinel, Wilson, Blumberg & Wheatley, 1998).
title: Forecasting a tenure disappointment
lens: the gap between predicted and recorded impact

sourceText: - **432.** Californians are no happier than Midwesterners, although both groups think they are (Schkade & Kahneman, 1998).
title: A climate-based happiness forecast
lens: the forecast error separate from a regional label

sourceText: - **433.** People with long commutes report lower life satisfaction, not offset by higher pay or cheaper housing (Stutzer & Frey, 2008).
title: The time spent commuting
lens: the weekly time budget behind a commute tradeoff

sourceText: - **434.** Among daily activities, commuting was rated least pleasant and socializing among the most (Kahneman, Krueger, Schkade, Schwarz & Stone, 2004).
title: A day is a mix of activities
lens: the time weights behind an average experience score

sourceText: - **435.** People's minds wander about 47% of the time, and they are less happy when they do (Killingsworth & Gilbert, 2010).
title: Forty-seven percent of sampled moments
lens: the sampled-moment denominator in a reported share

sourceText: - **436.** Unemployment lowers life satisfaction far more than lost income explains (Clark & Oswald, 1994), and people often don't fully recover (Lucas, Clark, Georgellis & Diener, 2004).
title: A persistent unemployment shock
lens: the persistence assumption rather than automatic full recovery

sourceText: - **437.** People are less happy when their neighbors earn more (Luttmer, 2005).
title: Income beside the neighbor's income
lens: the comparison reference with fixed own resources

sourceText: - **439.** People would rather wait a few days for a kiss from their favorite film star than have it now, to savor it (Loewenstein, 1987).
title: An anticipated reward and waiting
lens: the assumed value of a later option at different delays

sourceText: - **440.** People overestimate how bad they'll feel after losing a gamble (Kermer, Driver-Linn, Wilson & Gilbert, 2006).
title: Forecasting a lost gamble
lens: the gap between predicted and realized emotional impact

sourceText: - **442.** Across 90 studies, people forgo about three-quarters of what they could gain by lying (Abeler, Nosenzo & Raymond, 2019).
title: Forgone gains from dishonest reports
lens: the opportunity total behind a forgone fraction

sourceText: - **444.** An office bagel seller using an honor box was paid for about 87–90% of bagels (Levitt, 2006).
title: The honor-box payment share
lens: the denominator behind two recorded payment rates

sourceText: - **445.** About a third of buyers paid for honor-system newspapers in Austria; reminders of morality raised the amount paid (Pruckner & Sausgruber, 2013).
title: An honor-system newspaper
lens: quantity and payment receipts in a toy revenue example

sourceText: - **446.** **\[retracted\]** A study reported that signing an honesty pledge at the top of a form reduced cheating (Shu, Mazar, Gino, Ariely & Bazerman, 2012); it was retracted in 2021 after its field data were shown to be fabricated.
title: Exclude fabricated field records
lens: the evidential consequence of excluding invalid records

sourceText: - **447.** A large replication found signing first did not reduce dishonest reporting (Kristal et al., 2020).
title: Signing first: a null comparison
lens: zero versus a small descriptive standardized difference

sourceText: - **448.** **\[contested\]** Recalling the Ten Commandments was reported to reduce cheating (Mazar, Amir & Ariely, 2008), but a 25-lab replication found no effect (Verschuere et al., 2018).
title: One report and twenty-five labs
lens: the weight of larger replication collections

sourceText: - **449.** **\[contested\]** Bank employees reminded of their job cheated more on a coin-flip task (Cohn, Fehr & Maréchal, 2014); a later replication did not find it (Rahwan, Yoeli & Fasolo, 2019).
title: A professional-prime replication
lens: the evidence mix when a later estimate is near zero

sourceText: - **450.** Across 23 countries, higher national rates of corruption, tax evasion and fraud predicted more lying in a lab task (Gächter & Schulz, 2016).
title: Countries differ in composition
lens: an aggregate association without individual causal inference

sourceText: - **451.** Athens taxi drivers took longer routes with passengers who seemed unfamiliar with the city (Balafoutas, Beck, Kerschbamer & Sutter, 2013).
title: The unfamiliar passenger's route
lens: the additional bill for a specified route deviation

sourceText: - **452.** Swiss dentists recommended unnecessary treatment in about 28% of visits by a test patient (Gottschalk, Mimra & Waibel, 2020).
title: Unnecessary treatment visits
lens: the visit denominator behind a reported fraction

sourceText: - **453.** Auto mechanics recommended unneeded repairs to undercover customers (Schneider, 2012).
title: Repairs added to the estimate
lens: the complete bill with specified extra repairs

sourceText: - **455.** In the same study, letters threatening audits raised self-reported income (Kleven et al., 2011).
title: An audit changes expected cash
lens: the detection probability in an explicit payoff model

sourceText: - **456.** Call-center workers shirked more when they believed monitoring had been reduced (Nagin, Rebitzer, Sanders & Taylor, 2002).
title: Less monitoring changes the payoff
lens: the expected sanction when detection falls

sourceText: - **457.** Many people cheat a little but stop well short of the maximum, to keep a positive self-image (Mazar, Amir & Ariely, 2008).
title: Cheating below the maximum
lens: the realized amount relative to an explicit opportunity ceiling

sourceText: - **459.** UN diplomats from more corrupt countries racked up more unpaid New York parking tickets when they had immunity (Fisman & Miguel, 2007).
title: Parking fines with immunity
lens: the enforceability of a stated sanction

sourceText: - **460.** Teachers cheated on standardized tests in an estimated 4–5% of Chicago classrooms (Jacob & Levitt, 2003).
title: An estimated classroom share
lens: the count implied by the endpoints of a stated range

sourceText: - **461.** **\[contested\]** Thinking about a $1,500 car repair lowered poorer participants' test scores, and Indian sugarcane farmers scored higher after harvest than before (Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir & Zhao, 2013); a large replication did not find the effect (O'Donnell et al., 2021).
title: Scarcity and conflicting replications
lens: the influence of a larger replication set

sourceText: - **462.** Players made "poor" in lab games borrowed more and focused narrowly on immediate needs (Shah, Mullainathan & Shafir, 2012).
title: An immediate need meets borrowing
lens: the next-period debt from a stated short-term payment

sourceText: - **463.** US low-income households showed no drop in cognitive function before payday (Carvalho, Meier & Wang, 2016).
title: A payday comparison with no gap
lens: zero versus a small standardized descriptive gap

sourceText: - **465.** About 31% of social media use stems from self-control problems (Allcott, Gentzkow & Song, 2022).
title: A self-control share of screen time
lens: the total time behind a stated attributable share

sourceText: - **466.** Deactivating Facebook for four weeks modestly raised wellbeing and reduced political polarization (Allcott, Braghieri, Eichmeyer & Gentzkow, 2020).
title: Deactivation and a measured outcome
lens: the unit and spread behind a mean difference

sourceText: - **467.** **\[contested\]** Merely having a smartphone nearby was reported to reduce working memory (Ward, Duke, Gneezy & Bos, 2017); later replications mostly failed.
title: Phone presence and failed replications
lens: the study selection behind a reported cognitive effect

sourceText: - **468.** People memorizing a 7-digit number chose chocolate cake over fruit salad 63% of the time, versus 41% for those memorizing 2 digits (Shiv & Fedorikhin, 1999).
title: Digit load and cake choices
lens: the descriptive choice rates under stated conditions

sourceText: - **469.** **\[contested\]** Self-control was said to be a depletable resource (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven & Tice, 1998); a 23-lab replication found an effect near zero (Hagger et al., 2016).
title: Depletion meets twenty-three labs
lens: the evidence weight assigned to a near-zero replication

sourceText: - **471.** Higher scores on that test go with more patience and different risk attitudes (Frederick, 2005).
title: Reflection and a correlated attitude
lens: the explained share under a stated simple linear association

sourceText: - **472.** An extra hour of weekly sleep raises wages about 1% in the short run and 5% in the long run (Gibson & Shrader, 2018).
title: Sleep and two wage horizons
lens: two distinct relative changes on the same toy baseline

sourceText: - **474.** Higher fine-particle pollution on exam days lowered Israeli students' scores, with lasting effects on education and earnings (Ebenstein, Lavy & Roth, 2016).
title: Pollution and an exam-score contrast
lens: the score scale behind a standardized contrast

sourceText: - **475.** People overweight whichever attribute stands out most in a given comparison, salience theory (Bordalo, Gennaioli & Shleifer, 2012).
title: A salient attribute gets extra weight
lens: the weight assigned to a prominent attribute

sourceText: - **476.** Landlords read more about applicants with majority-sounding names, a form of "attention discrimination" (Bartoš, Bauer, Chytilová & Matějka, 2016).
title: Unequal attention to applications
lens: the reading time in a specified review process

sourceText: - **477.** Doctors order fewer cancer screenings as the clinic day goes on (Hsiang et al., 2019).
title: Screening later in a clinic day
lens: the reach of a stated screening funnel

sourceText: - **479.** Most people at risk for Huntington's disease avoid genetic testing, even though results would change their plans (Oster, Shoulson & Dorsey, 2013).
title: A test with an information cost
lens: the stated net value without prescribing a medical choice

sourceText: - **480.** People pay to avoid information that might be bad news (Golman, Hagmann & Loewenstein, 2017).
title: Paying to avoid bad news
lens: the cash cost of information avoidance

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **481.** "Power poses" were said to raise testosterone and risk-taking (Carney, Cuddy & Yap, 2010); a larger study found no hormonal or behavioral effect (Ranehill et al., 2015).
title: Power poses and later evidence
lens: the weight of a larger null replication

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **482.** A second, pre-registered multi-lab test of ego depletion also found an effect close to zero (Vohs et al., 2021).
title: Another depletion replication
lens: the sensitivity to a pre-specified replication collection

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **483.** Reading words about old age was said to make people walk slower (Bargh, Chen & Burrows, 1996); replications with automated timing failed (Doyen, Klein, Pichon & Cleeremans, 2012).
title: Automated timing and a walking claim
lens: the influence of later measurement-based replications

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **484.** Exposure to images of money was said to make people more selfish (Vohs, Mead & Goode, 2006); large replications, including Many Labs, found no effect (Rohrer, Pashler & Harris, 2015).
title: Money primes and larger studies
lens: the evidence mix behind a priming claim

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **485.** Thinking about professors was said to improve trivia scores (Dijksterhuis & van Knippenberg, 1998); a 23-lab replication found no effect (O'Donnell et al., 2018).
title: A trivia prime and twenty-three labs
lens: the weight of multi-lab replication evidence

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **486.** Holding a pen in the teeth to force a smile was said to make cartoons funnier (Strack, Martin & Stepper, 1988); a 17-lab replication found no effect (Wagenmakers et al., 2016), though later work found small effects in some setups (Coles et al., 2022).
title: Facial feedback across setups
lens: the sensitivity of an estimate to setup-specific later results

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **487.** Brian Wansink's food-psychology lab, source of findings on plate size and "bottomless" soup bowls, had about 18 papers retracted after data problems surfaced in 2017–18.
title: Retracted records leave the pool
lens: the usable-data denominator after invalid data are removed

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **488.** Self-control was said to depend on blood glucose (Gailliot et al., 2007); later work found no such link.
title: Glucose and a later null result
lens: the weight of later evidence on an initial link

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **493.** Thinking about past wrongdoing was said to make people want to wash, the "Macbeth effect" (Zhong & Liljenquist, 2006); replications failed (Earp, Everett, Madva & Hamlin, 2014).
title: A cleansing prime meets replication
lens: the study weights behind a failed-replication contrast

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **494.** Stereotype threat effects on women's math scores look small and inflated by publication bias (Flore & Wicherts, 2015).
title: Publication selection changes the mean
lens: a sensitivity analysis for unobserved less favorable results

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **495.** Growth-mindset interventions have weak effects on average (Sisk et al., 2018), with a national study finding about 0.1 grade points among lower-achieving students (Yeager et al., 2019).
title: A small effect in one subgroup
lens: the subgroup weights behind an average grade increment

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **496.** Hurricanes with female names were said to kill more people because they seemed less threatening (Jung, Shavitt, Viswanathan & Hilbe, 2014); critics showed the result hinged on a few outliers.
title: A few extreme storms move the mean
lens: the sensitivity of a mean to a specified extreme observation

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **497.** Moral licensing, where a good deed licenses a bad one, shrinks to near zero after correcting for publication bias (Kuper & Bott, 2019).
title: Licensing after selection adjustment
lens: the sensitivity of a pooled estimate to missing null results

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **498.** Several papers co-authored by Francesca Gino were retracted after a Harvard investigation concluded data had been falsified.
title: An invalid dataset is not evidence
lens: the denominator after excluding specified invalid records

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **499.** In Many Labs 1, anchoring, gain/loss framing, sunk costs and the gambler's fallacy replicated, while flag and money priming did not (Klein et al., 2014).
title: Replication needs a denominator
lens: the descriptive success share without a universal-effect claim

sourceSection: 25. Famous findings that failed to replicate or shrank
sourceText: - **500.** Implicit Association Test scores predict discriminatory behavior only weakly, r ≈ 0.15 (Oswald, Mitchell, Blanton, Jaccard & Tetlock, 2013).
title: A correlation of fifteen hundredths
lens: the explained share in a specified simple linear model
